text: Real analysis rarely lives in one table. Orders are in one place, customer details in another, and monthly files arrive separately. In SQL you combine tables with join and union all. pandas has the same two ideas: merge for joining side by side on a key, and concat for stacking tables on top of each other. You already know join types from T-SQL, so we won't re-teach them — the focus here is the pandas syntax and its specific pitfalls.

Merge orders onto customers on customer underscore id. The default is an inner join, so only rows with a match on both sides survive — customer 106, who has no orders, simply vanishes from the result. Notice the output is ordered by customer rather than by order, so don't assume merge preserves your original row order on an inner join.

The how argument selects the join type, using names you already know from SQL: inner, left, right, and outer. Merge customers onto orders with how equals left, and now all six customers appear, nine rows total — eight matched rows plus Fay Park with NaN in every order column. Also notice order underscore id became a decimal, 1.0, 3.0, because a whole-number column that receives a missing value gets converted to floats in pandas 1.x.

Add indicator equals True, and pandas creates a underscore merge column saying exactly where each row came from: both, left underscore only, or right underscore only. Filter for left underscore only, and you get back customer 106, Fay Park — the pandas version of a left join where right dot key is null, an anti-join, and a great way to audit any merge before you trust it.

If the key columns have different names, use left underscore on and right underscore on instead of on — both key columns are kept in the result. And if both tables have a non-key column with the same name, pandas appends underscore x and underscore y to tell them apart automatically — control that instead with suffixes, naming the clash something that actually means something, like underscore order and underscore cust.

Here's the silent killer: if the key is duplicated on the lookup side, each matching row gets repeated. If the customers table accidentally contained Ava Chen twice, merging orders onto it would return 10 rows instead of 8, and totals computed afterward would be quietly inflated — nothing raises an error on its own. The validate argument turns that into a loud error instead — passing validate equals m colon 1 raises a MergeError the moment the right side's keys aren't actually unique. Get in the habit of checking row counts before and after every merge, and of using validate.

Join is a shortcut for merging on the index instead of a named column. Set customer underscore id as the index on both orders and customers, then call dot-join, which defaults to a left join. Most people use merge for everything instead, because it's explicit about the key — and that's a perfectly fine rule to follow.

Use concat when tables share the same columns and you just want more rows, like union all. Split orders into a January piece and everything-after piece, then concat them back into a list — the result has all 8 rows again. Each piece keeps its original index labels by default, which can produce duplicates when pieces each start from 0 — add ignore underscore index equals True to renumber cleanly from 0. If the columns differ, concat keeps all of them and fills gaps with NaN, which is convenient but can hide a typo in a column name, so check dot-columns afterward.

A very common pattern: aggregate first, then merge the aggregate back onto another table. Group orders by customer underscore id, sum the amount, rename it to total, then merge that summary onto customers with how equals left. Fay Park gets NaN for total, since she has no orders — whether that should become 0 or stay missing is your call; for a total-spent report, you'd likely fill it with 0.

To recap: merge joins side by side with on and how, indicator equals True audits unmatched rows, validate prevents silent row multiplication, and concat stacks tables, ideally with ignore underscore index equals True. Always compare row counts before and after any merge. Next: reshaping with pivot and melt.
